Problem

POI 2013 MUL-Multidrink

Given a tree, you need to find a path from to that goes through every node, such that the distance between any two consecutive nodes is at most , or determine that it is impossible.

.

Sample:

Creativity/Observation:

Implementation:

Algorithms:

Beauty:

Solution

Denote a "path that goes through every node" as a Hamiltonian path, and a "Hamiltonian path such that the distance between any two consecutive nodes is at most " as a good path.

We need some observations.

Part 1

Let's root the tree at .

Since we need to find a path from to that goes through every node, we realize that the chain from to is very important. For every node not on this chain, we must leave the chain to visit it, and then leave the node to go back to the chain.

Observation : If we delete the chain from to , then the tree breaks into several subtrees.

For a subtree, we must enter it, traverse the whole subtree, and then exit back to the chain.

Also, there are only two ways to enter it, either from its root, or from a root's child.

If we enter it from the root, then we must exit it through a root's child.

If we enter it from a root's child, then we must exit it through a root.

By examining the graph above, we can come up with another observation:

Observation : The two ways of entering the tree are basically the same, we just need to construct one of them.

That is because if we reverse a path starting from the root and exiting from its child, we now have a valid path starting from its child and from the root.

So the question becomes: for each subtree, we must find a good path that starts from the root, and ends at a root's child.

Part 2

To solve this problem, as usual, we might first play with some samples.

Again, we will find some observations:

Observation : If a node's child is a leaf of the tree, then it doesn't matter.

This is because we can first ignore them, and then append them after after the traversal.

Observation : If a node has children that are not leaves, then a good path does not exist.

See the right diagram. We will see that there is no way to go back to the node's children after traversing the second non-leaf children.

Observation : A good path exists iff for every node in the tree, it only has at most one non-leaf child.

Such trees are commonly called "caterpillar" trees, which is a chain with nodes dangling to it.

Proof by observations and . Now we just need to construct such a good path.

This problem is much easier, as we can use recursion to find a solution!

Let's say we want to traverse the subtree rooted at .

  • Append .

  • If has a non-leaf children, then find a good path for the subtree rooted at that node.

  • Reverse the path and append the whole path.

  • Append all children of that are leaves.

For example, we can construct a good path like this:

Now, we have solved the problem for all subtrees when the chain from to is deleted. The remaining problem is how to connect all those paths together using the chain.

Part 3

Let's denote the chain from to is , where and .

If there is a good path, then if we only consider nodes on the chain, then it must traverse the chain in some order, like .

After a good while of playing with samples, I came up with this very incredible observation:

Observation : If a good path exists for the whole tree, then there exists a good path such that the chain is traversed in the order .

Since distances between consecutive nodes must be , so we can at most "jump" over node.

Let's say that in some good path, we jumped over the node , which means that we went from to .

Then, if we go on and visit or , then since we must come back to later, we are doomed because the path to is blocked.

So, we then must visit next. Then, of course, we must visit next. So we visited: in that order.

Let's say the whole path (also considering nodes outside of the chain) is .

Then we can construct a better good path as follows:

  • .

Which is basically reversing the middle part. It is easily proven that it still forms a good path.

Example:

Part 4

We can now simplify the problem even more:

We need to find a good path that goes through the chain from to in that order, and we already know how to deal with subtrees outside of the chain.

Again, let's denote the chain from to is , where and .

There are still questions remaining. Let's say we are at and we want to go to . How exactly do we traverse the whole subtree of and move on?

It is different from subtrees outside of the chain, as you don't need to go back to the root. Specifically, whether we enter the subtree by the root or by a root's children matters. Let's play with some samples.

Observation : If a root's child is a leaf, then it doesn't matter, if there exists at least one non-leaf child.

This is because we can append all the leaves either before that non-leaf child or after that non-leaf child, depending on whether its subtree has already been traversed.

Observation : If a root has no non-leaf child, then there exists a good path.

However:

  • If the current root has no leaf child also, then we can either enter the next root through itself or through its child.

  • Else if we enter the current root's subtree through the root, then we must enter the next root through itself.

  • Else if we enter the current root's subtree through a child, then we can either enter the next root through itself or through its child.

Observation : If a root has one non-leaf child, then there exists a good path.

However:

  • If we enter the current root's subtree through the root, then we must enter the next root through itself.

  • If we enter the current root's subtree through a child, then we can either enter the next root through itself or through its child.

Observation : If a root has two non-leaf children, then there exists a good path iff we enter through its children.

It can be verified that it is impossible if we enter through the root.

Also, if we enter the current root's subtree through the root, then we must enter the next root through the root.

Observation : If a root has non-leaf children, then there does not exist a good path.

Proof by looking at the picture above.

To summarize, the only difference between entering the root through itself or through its child is when it has two non-leaf children.

In that case, we should better enter the subtree through a root's child. Hence:

Observation : Entering a subtree through a root's child is strictly better than entering through the root.

Specifically, in observation and , if we enter the root's subtree through a child, then we should greedily enter the next root through its child.

That brings us to the construction to the good path. We just need to construct it as the picture above. And if our greedy strategy doesn't work, then output impossible.

Part 5

One last thing - what if the current node is , which we don't have a next node?

If is a leaf node, then we are done. Else, we must enter the subtree by its child (because we should visit last), and then we can view it as a normal subtree.

And we are done and ready to write some code.

Conclusion

It should be noted that there is also more solutions to this problem on Luogu, including a DP solution and some other crazy solutions that wrote lines of code.

In this problem, there are several takeaways:

  • Hard problems sometimes need a lot of observations. Make more observations by playing with samples or using logical/calculation deduction.

  • In tree/DP problems, it is common to group possibilities together as a state and analyze the state as a whole when making observations.

  • Problems can be converted into small, easier problems. Solving them can provide a partial solution to the whole problem.

  • It is even better to think quickly, but this probably takes practice.

Solution

Part 1

We color the unmovable monuments RED and the movable monuments BLUE.

Obviously, we can delete the RED monuments that are already symmetrical or at position . If the number of RED monuments is greater than the number of BLUE monuments, then it is impossible to match. Then every one of the rest of the RED monuments must be matched with one BLUE monument, and the rest must all be symmetrical BLUE monuments.

If the total number of monuments now is odd, then the number of the rest BLUE movable monuments is odd, hence at least one is at position . To simplify, we can add a RED monument at position and pretend this case doesn't happen.

If , then we must match exactly UPs with UPs or DOWNs with DOWNs.

New problem: Given a bipartite graph with left nodes at position and right nodes at position . Each node can be RED or BLUE. The cost to match with is , but if both nodes are RED, then you can't match it. Find the minimum complete bipartite matching cost.

Of course, we sort the left nodes and the right nodes. From the graph above, we see that we can split the matching into minimal segments such that for each segment, the left nodes and the right nodes in the segment still forms a complete bipartite matching.

Those who have already ACed [IOI 2017] Wiring might make the following critical observation:

  • Each segment must either: (1) consist of an equal number of RED and BLUE nodes, or (2) be a length- segment consisting of BLUE nodes.

Let's prove it. If a minimal segment consists of unequal number of RED and BLUE nodes, then obviously the number of BLUE nodes is greater than the number of RED nodes.

Hence, there must be a BLUE-BLUE match in this minimal segment. The two BLUE nodes split the left nodes and the right nodes into four different areas, let's say they are (as in picture).
